# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This follow-up answers several questions left open by the earlier documents:
- **Measurement:** it adds log-based hours to check whether timesheets missed work.
- **Duration:** it gives the first controlled estimate at 24 months.
- **Mechanism:** it registers the mediation analysis before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **Prior claims:** it addresses the earlier claims directly.

It also substantiates the duration critique I raised about the meta-analysis. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

The arithmetic checks:
- Per-hour gain on timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 gives **+9.8%**.
- Per-hour gain on logs: 0.966 / 0.89 gives **+8.5%**.
- Halden subset hours: 34.9 / 40.3 gives **−13.4%**.
- Halden subset per-hour gain: 0.968 / 0.866 gives **+11.8%**.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- Counter-arm cost: 12% more staff giving +9% cost per contact is consistent if staff are about 75% of costs. That assumption should be stated.

The issues below are mostly about what the new results mean, not about errors.

## 1. Two control offices cut their meetings, which biases the 24-month estimate

The "unplanned observation" is presented as suggestive evidence about reorganisation. It is also **contamination of the control arm**. Two of seven control offices cut their meetings at month 15. Their output per hour then rose about 4% over their own prior period. That raises the control benchmark and shrinks the measured treatment effect.

Consequences:
- **The estimated effect is biased downward.** The 24-month treatment effect is probably understated.
- **The apparent decline may not be all fading.** Some of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% could be the control arm improving rather than the treatment effect fading.
- **A sensitivity analysis is needed.** Report the 24-month estimates with those two offices excluded, or with only their pre-month-15 data. Also check whether other control offices changed their practices.

This sits awkwardly with section 5, which uses the decline as the key evidence of decay.

## 2. The meeting arithmetic suggests the mediation shares understate meetings

Assume meeting time is counted in timesheet hours and produces no case output. Then:

| | Baseline | Month 24 |
|---|---|---|
| Timesheet hours | 37.9 | about 33.4 (−12%) |
| Recurring meetings | 7.4 | 3.9 |
| Non-meeting working time | 30.5 | 29.5 (**about −3%**) |

Output per FTE fell 3.4%. So **output per non-meeting hour is essentially unchanged**. On this accounting, removing meetings could explain nearly all of the per-hour gain, not 47%. That leaves little room for the 18% attributed to fatigue or the 35% left unexplained.

There are several ways this could be reconciled, and the paper should say which applies:
- **Definition of log hours.** If log hours count only active case-system time and exclude meetings, then the log and timesheet measures are not like-for-like. If meetings were cut by 3.5 hours, case time should then have fallen much less than 11%. If log hours do include meetings, "active log-in time" needs a clearer definition.
- **Additivity of the shares.** Meetings and fatigue are probably linked, since fewer meetings may reduce fatigue. Shares from separate mediator models do not necessarily add to 100%. How was the joint model specified?
- **A partly mechanical result.** Meeting hours are part of the per-hour denominator. Part of the meetings pathway is then an accounting identity rather than a behavioural mechanism. That is still important for policy, but it should be described as such.

## 3. Mediation: "confirms" is too strong

- **The test reuses the same offices.** The hypothesis came from these offices at month 6 and is now tested on them at month 24. This is a pre-specified test, which is real progress, but it is not an independent replication.
- **The sample is still small.** Treatment was assigned to 14 offices. Office-months are not independent units for a treatment assigned at office level. Intervals of 28–66% look narrow for 14 clusters. The paper should state how clustering was handled, preferably with a small-sample method such as the wild cluster bootstrap I raised for the nine-month report.
- **Confounding remains possible.** The Limitations note the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. A manager who is effective in other ways may also cut meetings.

"Supports" or "is consistent with" would be more accurate than "confirms". The improvement over the nine-month analysis still stands: there is now baseline meeting data and a control-arm comparison (7.4 → 3.9 treated, 7.2 → 7.0 control).

## 4. Other Varden points

- **The Summary compares two different hours measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". The 12.5% is a timesheet figure. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, as the body correctly says.
- **Two time points are not a trajectory.** Report the monthly or quarterly effect. Two points can't show whether the gain is levelling off or still falling.
- **Earlier outcome requests are still missing.** Backlog size, deadline compliance, and cost per case including overtime are not reported, though they are in county systems. Backlog would be most likely to show up at 24 months.
- **Some wellbeing and quality figures lack intervals.** Sick days (−27%), resignations, and appeal overturns have no confidence intervals. Sick days are still counted per FTE rather than per scheduled day.

## 5. Halden subset

The authors handle this well. They call the result an upper bound for organisations that chose reduced hours and found it suited them. Three points:

- **The baseline may be wrong for these 11.** The baseline of 40.3 hours exactly matches Varga & Holm's mean for all 27 organisations with time tracking. The 11 continuing organisations should be compared against their *own* baseline hours.
- **Non-response is likely selective.** Nine of 23 did not respond, and they are likely to have worse results.
- **The Summary's description of the reverters is too neat.** It says all three had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But the marketing agency cited *client deadlines*. That is deadline-driven work, which the meta-analysis classifies as discretionary. So one reverter was a discretionary organisation, and the Summary's framing hides that.

## 6. Authorship and framing

One author is from the Halden Institute, and the Varden authors are reporting on a hypothesis they proposed. Neither is a problem in itself, since the analyses were registered. But some phrases are written as rebuttal, such as "since dismissed as post hoc" and "confirms". A more neutral tone would strengthen the paper.

## 7. Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work, rigorous measurement | **About 8.5–10% at 24 months** (one public employer, 7 v 7 offices); possibly understated because of control contamination |
| Does it fade? | Partly. About a quarter on like-for-like measures, though contamination may account for some of this. It has not disappeared, so a pure novelty explanation is unlikely |
| Output per worker, discretionary | **About −3%** (interval includes zero). This is the cost of the hours cut |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fell enough that the county ended the arm. Restoring service would cost about 9% more per contact |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings is the leading candidate, possibly larger than 47%. Fatigue plays a smaller role |
| Gain without cutting hours? | **Open, and now the key policy question.** Two control offices suggest some of the gain is available through reorganisation alone. No arm tested this |

## Bottom line

This is the strongest single piece of evidence so far. It rules out "entirely an artifact" and "no decay". The most important open question has also shifted. If most of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value meetings, then an employer could capture much of it without cutting hours. What a reduced week then adds is chiefly the wellbeing and retention benefits, plus its role as a "forcing device" for reorganisation. That is roughly a 3% cost in output per worker.

The obvious next study is a three-arm trial:
- reduced hours;
- reorganisation with standard hours;
- control.

Before that, the authors should:
1. Re-estimate the 24-month effects excluding the contaminated control offices.
2. Clarify what log hours measure and reconcile it with the meeting arithmetic.
3. Fix the like-for-like comparison in the Summary.
